The study employs time-frequency analysis to dissect neuromuscular activation during the instep kick, distinguishing between two distinct phases—pre-contact (Phase 1) and post-contact (Phase 2). This dual-phase structure allows for the identification of skill-level differences in activation timing and spectral content. Principal component analysis (PCA) reduces dimensionality of multi-muscle sEMG data, revealing that elite and amateur players exhibit distinct neuromuscular strategies. Specifically, elite players show a more temporally focused pre-contact activation centered on mid-frequency components of the biceps femoris, while amateurs rely more heavily on higher-frequency components of the medial gastrocnemius during the follow-through. These findings suggest that skill is not merely reflected in overall activation magnitude but in the precise temporal and spectral organization of muscle activity within critical time windows. The use of Morlet wavelets ensures localized time-frequency resolution, enabling detection of transient activation patterns missed by traditional methods. Statistical significance is established via SPM1D t-tests on PC trajectories, adjusting for multiple comparisons. This approach supports a mechanistic understanding of how skilled motor control emerges from fine-tuned neuromuscular coordination.
